keyVerseText: Therefore all they that devour thee shall be devoured; and all thine adversaries, every one of them, shall go into captivity; and they that spoil thee shall be a spoil, and all that prey upon thee will I give for a prey.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb שָׁאַס (shâʼaç) is a primitive root that fundamentally conveys the action of spoiling or plundering. Its core sense involves the violent or forceful taking of goods or possessions, emphasizing destruction and loss. This literal sense of stripping away or ravaging adds a depth beyond the simple English gloss 'spoil,' highlighting the aggressive and devastating nature of the act.
usageInScripture: This verb appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Jeremiah 30:16, where it is translated as 'and they that spoil.' The consistency in its translation as 'spoil' or 'plunder' underscores its clear and focused semantic range, emphasizing the act of forceful despoiling. This singular usage suggests a strong thematic role in the context of judgment and reversal of fortunes described in the passage.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding שָׁאַס as an act of plundering or spoiling enriches our grasp of divine judgment and justice in Scripture. It conveys the reality of consequences for those who oppose God’s people, reflecting the seriousness with which God addresses injustice and harm. From a Christ-centered perspective, this word reminds believers of the ultimate victory over forces that seek to destroy or despoil the people of God. It also points to the hope of restoration, where those who once plundered will themselves become subject to God’s righteous judgment, affirming His sovereignty and faithfulness to His covenant.
keyVerseReflection: Jeremiah 30:16 declares, 'Therefore all they that devour thee shall be devoured; and all thine adversaries, every one of them, shall go into captivity; and they that spoil thee shall be a spoil.' Here, שָׁאַס highlights the fate of those who violently take from God's people—they themselves will be despoiled. This word intensifies the verse’s message of reversal, assuring that the oppressors’ destructive actions will be met with divine recompense, reinforcing God’s protective and just nature.
